Recording rides for comparison

Source: vignettes/recording_rides.Rmd
recording_rides.Rmd

Everything in vignette("cyclingpower") assumes you already have two or three files recorded from the same riding. Getting those files is where it goes wrong, and most of the ways it goes wrong cannot be repaired afterwards: a dropped sample is gone, a mid-ride auto-pause cannot be undone, and a perfectly steady hour contains no evidence about how far apart the head unit clocks were.

This vignette is the recording protocol. Following it costs one extra minute at the start of a ride.

There are two routes, and most of what can go wrong belongs to only one of them. launch_app() can record the meters itself over Web Bluetooth, in which case one clock stamps every sample and half the failures below cannot happen. Where that is not possible — an ANT+-only meter, a browser other than Chrome or Edge — each meter keeps its own head unit and the recordings are independent, which is the case the rest of this vignette is mostly about.

Recording in the app

Open the app, go to the Record tab, and pair each meter. What that buys is a single timebase: the page stamps every sample from its own clock at the moment it arrives, so the sources share a clock by construction rather than having one recovered from them afterwards. Auto-pause, smart recording and an unset head unit clock are all failure modes of independent recorders, and none of them exists here.

Four constraints come with it. Settle all four before the ride.

Chrome or Edge. Safari has never shipped Web Bluetooth and WebKit has no active bug for it; Mozilla declined the specification on privacy grounds. The Record tab detects this and says so rather than offering a button that silently does nothing. http://localhost counts as a secure context, so nothing has to be done about certificates.

One press per meter. The browser will not open its device chooser programmatically, so pairing three meters is three presses. There is no way round it.

A meter holds one Bluetooth connection at a time. While the page has the trainer, Zwift and TrainerRoad cannot. Pair the training app to the trainer over ANT+ instead — a dual-band trainer takes FE-C control over ANT+ and broadcasts power over BLE simultaneously, so the training app drives the targets while the recorder listens. If your erg targets are being commanded over Bluetooth, they will stop the moment you pair the trainer here.

Leave the tab visible. Chrome throttles background tabs and stalls notifications on a sleeping display. The app holds a screen wake lock while recording and reacquires it when the tab comes back, but a tab buried behind a training app is not something the wake lock helps with.

The app writes <run>_<source>.csv per meter into the directory you choose, appending and flushing each batch as it arrives, so a browser tab that dies mid-ride costs a fraction of a second rather than the ride. Both labels become filenames, so they take letters, digits and hyphens only, and an existing file is never written over. When you stop, the Rides tab scans that directory like any other: the handoff between the recorder and the analysis is the filesystem and nothing else.

A meter that drops out is shown as disconnected and reconnected automatically. The seconds it missed are a gap in its file, not a run of zeros. Zeros would be read as coasting, and coasting is dropped as a second both meters agreed on, so a lost connection would enter the comparison as evidence of agreement.

One caveat. The packet parser is unit-tested against captured byte arrays, and the file writing is tested end to end through the same pipeline every other ride goes through. The radio path — the chooser, the GATT connection, notifications, the reconnection loop — is not tested and cannot be without a physical meter. Ride the first session against a head unit you already trust and compare the two files before relying on the app for anything you care about.

What to ride when the app is recording

The separate-head-unit route below asks for surges because the cross-correlation needs an edge to lock onto, and steps because the by-level comparison needs coverage. Once one clock stamps every sample the offset is zero by construction and that compromise dissolves: erg mode becomes the best ride rather than the worst, because it puts a chosen number of seconds into a chosen band instead of leaving band coverage to how the day went.

One piece has to survive. With no feature to lock onto, check_alignment() cannot tell “these clocks agree” from “these traces cannot be compared at all”: it collapses both into unresolved, forces the offset to zero and warns. A recorder that stamped every meter wrongly would pass that check exactly as a correct one does. So a short sync block stays — not to find the offset, but to make finding it possible, so that a resolved zero is evidence rather than a default.

Block Duration Mode Target Why
Zero and settle 30 s — Coasting A shared floor of true zeros at the head of every file
Sync surges 4 × (8 s / 20 s) Level or slope About 375 W, coasting between Coast-to-power edges, so check_alignment() can resolve rather than default
Ladder up 5 × 2 min Erg 138 W → 175 W → 212 W → 250 W → 275 W Several hundred stable seconds in each band
Coast 1 min — Coasting Exercises the coasting drop
Ladder down 5 × 2 min Erg 275 W → 250 W → 212 W → 175 W → 138 W The same bands, later in the ride
Stop together 30 s — Coasting A shared tail
Total 24 min Ride it the same way every time. Chained comparisons assume the bridge meter reads the same on both days

The targets above are for a 250 W rider; collapse_protocol() takes your own FTP. Twenty-four minutes, which is short enough to ride twice in a session when you are chaining a third meter. Ride it identically every time, because a chained comparison rests on the bridge meter reading the same in both runs and chain_report()$overlap can only confirm the two runs covered the same power if they were asked to.

Two minutes a step is a floor, not a default to trim. What runs out first is not min_seconds but bootstrap blocks. The up and down ladders land in the same bands, so a band carries roughly twice the step length, and at a 60-second block two-minute steps leave it about four blocks to resample. Going shorter drops under three, and a bootstrap drawing two blocks is not estimating anything. The cost of getting here from four-minute steps is about 17% wider bands, measured on synthetic rides with a planted gain. That was a good trade for halving the session; going shorter again is not.

There is no sync block at the end. A closing block detects only a clock that drifted during the ride, and when the app records there is one clock stamping every meter, which cannot drift relative to itself. Independent head units are the case where two clocks can separate, and that route — below — should still repeat the surges at the end.

That table is comparison_protocol(), and write_workout() turns it into a file your training app can command, so “identically every time” is something the trainer does rather than something you remember. The Record tab has the same table and a download button on it.

write_workout("comparison.zwo", ftp = 250)

A .zwo writes the ladder steps as SteadyState and the surges and coasts as FreeRide, which drops the trainer out of erg for exactly the blocks that must not be ridden in it. A .erg course — Golden Cheetah, TrainerDay, PerfPro — has no way to express that, so it carries the surge targets as watts and you switch out of erg by hand. Either file is loaded into the training app, which commands the trainer over ANT+ while this page holds its Bluetooth.

The ladder runs up and then back down. A meter reading high because it has warmed up gives different numbers at the same target on the way down; a level-dependent meter repeats itself. Ridden in one direction only the two are indistinguishable, and level_dependence() would report the drift as an error that depends on power.

Do not surge in erg. The trainer fights the surge and rounds off precisely the edge the cross-correlation needs. Switch to level or slope mode for the sync blocks.

Erg makes the trainer the controlled variable, holding its own reading at target, so within a step the trainer is nearly flat and almost all the spread comes from the other meter. That does not bias anything — level is the mean of the two, not the trainer’s number — but it does mean the trainer decides which band a second lands in, rather than both meters having wandered into that band together.

Hold a steady cadence through each step. If you want one extra thing from the session, repeat a single step at two cadences perhaps 25 rpm apart: a crank or pedal meter’s error can depend on cadence, and the channel is carried through the schema, though nothing in the package looks at it yet.

Driving it from a head unit

A head unit is the easiest thing to put on the other end, and on a Wahoo ELEMNT, BOLT or ROAM the workout can be pushed to it from intervals.icu, which imports .zwo directly. Three things to settle before the ride; two of them are silent when they go wrong.

Force the head unit to pair the trainer over ANT+. An ELEMNT connects to a Wahoo trainer over Bluetooth by default, and pairing it that way spends the Bluetooth connection this page needs. Wahoo’s own instruction for using the trainer with another app at the same time is to force the ANT+ pairing, and a head unit controlling over FE-C leaves the Bluetooth side untouched. A KICKR or CORE on firmware from late 2019 onwards will hold three Bluetooth connections and may appear to tolerate both, but two controllers on one radio is not a thing to build a session on.

A block with no power target releases erg by itself. In planned-workout mode the head unit follows the workout’s own resistance design, and a segment carrying no target drops the trainer into resistance mode rather than holding the last one. That is what the sync surges need, so the FreeRide blocks come out right without anything being switched by hand.

The workout and the recording are independent. The head unit commands the trainer; this page records; nothing passes between them. So the sync block only has to be in the recording, not in the workout — if the surges arrive as erg targets anyway, ride them in level mode before starting the workout and the comparison cannot tell the difference. Exploit that on the first session: the head unit is recording the ride regardless, so its own file of the trainer against this page’s file of the same trainer is a free check on the one path in the recorder that has no automated test.

One meter, many listeners

Everything from here is the other route: one head unit per meter, recordings that are independent, and a clock offset that has to be recovered from the power traces afterwards. It is what an ANT+-only meter needs, and what to fall back on when the app cannot record.

The constraint that shapes the whole setup is that a power meter broadcasts, but a recorder records one power source. There is no consumer head unit that writes two power channels into an ordinary file.

Over ANT+ that is not a problem. ANT+ is a one-to-many broadcast with no handshake, so a single meter can be picked up by any number of head units at once, and two head units listening to the same meter do not interfere with each other. Bluetooth is a connection rather than a broadcast, and classically a meter accepted one at a time; recent firmware on many meters allows two, but you cannot rely on it.

The practical rule follows: pair each meter to its own recorder over ANT+ wherever the meter offers it, and keep Bluetooth for the one device that has no ANT+ radio — usually a phone or a computer running Zwift. Do not pair the same meter to two apps over Bluetooth and hope; the second connection will either be refused or will drop out intermittently, and intermittent drop-outs are much harder to spot in the file than a flat refusal.

So two meters need two recorders, and three meters need three. Common combinations:

Meters Recorders
Trainer + pedals Zwift (trainer, over Bluetooth) and a head unit (pedals, over ANT+)
Two bike-mounted meters Two head units, both over ANT+
Three meters Two head units plus a phone app, or two runs and a bridge meter — see below

Two head units of the same model are marginally better than two different ones, because they will resolve and log the broadcast the same way. It is not important enough to buy one for.

Settings on each recorder

Three settings matter, the first two a great deal.

Record every second, not “smart” recording. Garmin’s smart recording writes a sample only when the numbers change enough, which produces a file with irregular gaps. align_rides() resamples onto a one-second grid and leaves unrecorded seconds empty, so smart recording thins the series that the cross-correlation and the per-second differencing both work on. This is the single most damaging setting on the head unit, and it is on by default on some units.

Turn auto-pause off on every recorder. align_rides() estimates one clock offset per source per run. An auto-pause that triggers on one unit and not the other — at a junction, or when the trainer drops below the speed threshold — shifts everything after it by the length of the pause, so the true offset becomes two different numbers and no single correction fixes both. A stopped period recorded as zeros is fine; the coasting seconds are dropped from the agreement anyway.

Let the clocks set themselves. Head units take their clock from GPS, and two units that both have a fix will usually be within a second or two of each other. A unit ridden indoors without a fix can be minutes out, and align_rides() only searches ±30 seconds by default. If you ride indoors, take each unit outside for a minute before you start, or raise max_offset.

Beyond that: start and stop both recorders as close together as you can manage, and if you are in a busy gym, keep each head unit near its meter, since ANT+ drop-outs from a crowded band show up as missing seconds in one file only.

Calibrating before you start

Do a zero offset on every meter, following the manufacturer’s instructions, immediately before each run and after a few minutes of easy pedalling — most meters drift with temperature, and a meter that has been in a cold garage will read differently over the first ten minutes than it does later.

Do not re-zero one meter mid-ride. A step change in one series and not the other is not something the analysis models: it will average the before and after into a single bias, and the limits of agreement will widen without any indication of why.

What to ride on separate head units

Two things the analysis needs pull in opposite directions. It is the compromise the app’s single clock dissolves, so if you are recording in the app, ride the session in the table above instead.

The alignment needs features. align_rides() recovers each clock offset by sliding one power trace against another and taking the offset with the highest correlation. A block at constant power correlates about equally well at every offset, so there is no peak to find, and check_alignment() returns unresolved, forces the offset to zero and warns. So a clean ERG session — the most controlled ride you can do — is the worst possible ride for establishing what the offset was.

The by-level comparison needs coverage. agreement_by_level() bins seconds by the mean of the two readings, so a bin only exists if you spent time there. Two hundred seconds at 250 W tells you about the meters at 250 W and nothing about them at 400 W.

So structure the run in two parts.

Start with a synchronisation block. Four to six sharp surges — eight to ten seconds well above your average for the day — each separated by about thirty seconds of soft pedalling or, better, complete coasting. Coast-to-power transitions are the sharpest edges available and are exactly what the cross-correlation locks onto. The coasting seconds are then dropped from the agreement calculation, so this block costs you nothing in the comparison. It takes about four minutes.

Then ride steps. Choose five or six targets spanning the range you care about — something like 55, 70, 85, 100 and 110 per cent of FTP — and hold each for four to five minutes. Steps are better than a ramp: a ramp sweeps every bin but leaves each one with a handful of transient seconds, recorded while both meters were still responding to a change, and meters respond at different speeds. Each step instead fills one or two bins with a few hundred stable seconds, and the transitions between steps populate the bins in between.

Repeat the synchronisation block at the end if the session is longer than an hour. It is not needed for the alignment, but it lets you check for clock drift: align the first ten minutes and the last ten minutes separately, and if the two offsets differ, one unit’s clock moved during the ride and a single constant correction is not enough for that file.

Comparing a trainer against a bike-mounted meter

A crank, spider or pedal meter measures power at the pedals; a trainer or hub measures it after the chain has been through the drivetrain. The difference is real, typically two to four per cent, and it is not disagreement between the meters — it is the transmission.

Nothing in the package knows this. power_agreement() will report a gain_pc of a few per cent for a pair of perfectly accurate devices in that configuration, so read the number net of an expected drivetrain loss rather than as pure measurement error. A clean drivetrain in a straight chainline sits at the low end of the range and a worn one at the high end, which is itself a reason not to try to pin the figure down too precisely.

Two bike-mounted meters do not have this problem, and pedals against a crank-based meter differ by only the bottom-bracket bearings, which is small enough to ignore.

Three meters and two recorders

If you have three meters but can only record two at a time, ride two sessions with one meter common to both: run one carries A and B, run two carries B and C. B is the bridge, and chain_sources() gets A against C from the two gains relative to B.

That comparison rests on B having read identically on both days, which the ride files cannot test, so the protocol is about protecting the assumption:

  • Ride the two runs as close together as you can — back to back on the same day is much better than a week apart.
  • Change nothing about B in between. No reinstallation, no battery change, no firmware update, no crank-length or scale-factor edits.
  • Cover the same power range in both runs. Use the same step targets, not just a similar overall effort. A gain estimated at endurance pace in one run and at threshold in the other is not really the same quantity.
  • Keep the conditions comparable, particularly temperature.

chain_report() reports what can be checked — the overlap in power range between the runs — and states the assumption in the output. Keep that statement wherever the numbers go.

Getting the files out and named

Export from each device as FIT where you can. GPX works, but Strava’s GPX export only carries power that a meter actually recorded: power Strava estimated from speed and gradient is not in the file, so a ride recorded without a meter arrives with no power channel at all, which is an error rather than a column of NA.

Name each file <run>_<source>, where the run is the session and the source is the meter:

rides/
  run1_kickr.fit
  run1_assioma.fit
  run2_assioma.fit
  run2_quarq.fit

Then ride_spec_from_names() builds the table read_rides() wants, and a filename that does not split cleanly is an error rather than a silently mislabelled ride.

library(cyclingpower)

aligned <- list.files("rides", full.names = TRUE) |>
  ride_spec_from_names() |>
  read_rides() |>
  align_rides()

Checking that the recording worked

Three checks before you trust anything downstream, all of them while you could still repeat the ride.

The alignment resolved:

alignment_report(aligned)

Every source should have status of aligned, and the offset should be a few seconds. An unresolved status means the synchronisation block was too soft or is missing; a large correlation with a large offset means the clocks really were far apart, which is fine. A low correlation on a ride you know had surges in it usually means the two files are not the same session.

For a ride the app recorded, look for aligned with an offset of zero, not an offset of zero on its own. unresolved returns zero too, and means the check could not be made.

The bins are populated:

agreement_by_level(aligned) |>
  dplyr::select(source_a, source_b, band_range, seconds, bias_w)

A bin resting on twenty seconds is not evidence of anything, and the steps are what fill the bins you care about.

And, for a chained comparison, that the two runs covered comparable ground:

chain_report(chain_sources(aligned))$coverage

The short version

Recording in the app, in Chrome:

  • Pair each meter on the Record tab, one press each, and label them.
  • Command erg targets over ANT+; the page holds the trainer’s Bluetooth.
  • Zero every meter, then thirty seconds still.
  • Four coast-to-sprint surges in level mode, so the alignment can resolve.
  • The ladder in erg, up and then back down through the same targets.
  • Sit still for thirty seconds, then stop every meter at once.
  • Check alignment_report() shows aligned, not merely an offset of zero.

Recording on separate head units:

  • One recorder per meter; ANT+ where the meter offers it.
  • One-second recording, auto-pause off, clocks set from GPS.
  • Zero every meter after a warm-up, immediately before the run.
  • Open with four to six coast-to-sprint surges so the alignment has something to lock onto.
  • Then five or six steady steps across the range you want to report on.
  • Expect a trainer to read two to four per cent below a pedal or crank meter.
  • Name the files <run>_<source> and check alignment_report() first.
